description_full: The Scotts Miracle-Gro Company, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacture, marketing, and sale of products for lawn, garden care, and indoor and hydroponic gardening in the United States and internationally. The company provides lawn care products, comprising lawn fertilizers, clover and grass seed products, spreaders, and other durable products, as well as lawn-related weed, pest, and disease control products; and gardening and landscape products, which include water-soluble and continuous-release plant foods, potting mixes, garden soils, mulches and ground cover products, plant-related pest and disease control products, organic garden products, and live goods and seeding solutions. It also offers hydroponic products that help users to grow plants, flowers, and vegetables using little or no soil; lighting systems and components; insect, rodent, and weed control products for home areas; and non-selective weed killer products. The company sells its products under the Scotts, Turf Builder, Grower's Edge, EZ Seed, PatchMaster, Thick'R Lawn, GrubEx, EdgeGuard, Whirl, Wizz, Miracle-Gro, LiquaFeed, Shake N Feed, Hyponex, Earthgro, Miracle-Gro Organic, CAN-FAN, CAN-FILTERS, EcoPlus, Bug B Gon, Nature Scapes, Ortho, Miracle-Gro Performance Organics, Miracle-Gro Organic Choice, Whitney Farms, Ortho Max, Home Defense, Mother Earth, Botanicare, General Hydroponics, CYCO, Gavita, Agrolux, HydroLogic Purification System, Gro Pro, AeroGarden, Titan, Tomcat, Ortho Weed B Gon, Roundup, Groundclear, and Alchemist brands. It serves home centers, mass merchandisers, warehouse clubs, large hardware chains, independent hardware stores, nurseries, garden centers, e-commerce platforms, and food and drug stores, as well as indoor gardening and hydroponic distributors, retailers, and growers. The company was formerly known as The Scotts Company. The Scotts Miracle-Gro Company was founded in 1868 and is headquartered in Marysville, Ohio.

financial_summary: Scotts Miracle-Gro Company (The is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $3.4B market cap on $3.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -5% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 33%.

The business throws off $274M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.56× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 24% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 11% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.81x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-17.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 222 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 11% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 1.17, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.03 vs 5y 1.28), so read it loosely.
About $54.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 38% in the 2020 crash, 75% in the 2022 bear market and 58% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $47.76 (margin of safety -23%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $28.40 to $77.30 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Basic Materials peers: cheaper on P/FCF 12.5 vs 20.4, richer on P/E 17.8 vs 14.2 and EV/EBITDA 10.6 vs 7.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 12% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 8.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $76.33 on average, 30% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 8.3%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.72).
It runs a 33% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.56x.
It spends 1.0% of revenue on R&D and 2.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.9x net debt to EBITDA ($36.6M of cash against $2.1B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.8x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -4.5% over 3 years, -3.7% over 5 years and 1.2% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
At current returns, reinvesting 2% of profits supports about 0.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -11.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (2.9% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 2, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 12.6% on average.
own: Insiders own 23.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 88%.
It returns 5.1% a year to shareholders (0.5% in buybacks and 4.5% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 20 consecutive years, though it has been cut 17.8% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 11.5% of the float, 4.9 days to cover.
